notes.note: The definition the whole course is built on. Keep McCall's two halves apart: a research object ('the study of islands') and a political stance ('on their own terms').
notes.quote: defined nissology as the study of islands on their own terms

notes.note: The prepositions carry the argument: of, by, with, for. Try them on our case studies. Kench et al. (Tuvalu) write about islanders; who writes with them?
notes.quote: not as a pursuit by islands/islanders, or with them

notes.note: Scale check: about 7% of land and about 10% of people, excluding the continents. Islands are not marginal in total, only individually.
notes.quote: islands cover some 7% of the Earth

notes.note: McCall's provocation: emigration and diaspora are so central to island life that islands 'defy territoriality'. Think of Pitcairn's 1856 move to Norfolk Island, or Tristan's 1961 evacuation to England.

notes.note: Signpost for the paper's core. The five: colonial loyalty, disclosure, language, victimhood, and 'we are all imperialists'.

notes.note: Thesis of the second half: the clear edges of islands make them easy to idealise as model societies or eco-laboratories.

notes.note: Useful vocabulary. Surtsey is locus (a natural laboratory for succession); Pitcairn's Bounty history is focus (the island's own story).

notes.quote: explorer-discoverer-colonist

notes.note: Island studies is a field with many disciplines inside it. This course uses geomorphology, ecology, genetics, archaeology and political geography, and that mix is normal for the field.
notes.quote: we are dealing less with a discipline than with multiple approaches to a single field

notes.note: A sampling bias in the field itself. Check our own list: no South-east Asian or Russian island. What would a Philippine or Kuril case study add?

notes.note: The key methodological argument. Generalising from Saint Helena or Nauru is as biased as generalising from Manhattan. Our six islands are all remote, so be careful which conclusions you draw from them.

notes.note: Farbotko's term, applied to 'sinking' Tuvalu. Compare Kench et al. (2018), who say messages of inevitable loss have 'normalised island loss'.

notes.note: The ethical recommendation: be sceptical of the claimed benefits of islandness, for example sustainability branding or 'offshoring' of controversial activities.
notes.quote: nurture a healthy scepticism

notes.note: Physical geography in an essay: glacio-isostatic rebound. Islands change size through tectonics (Henderson's uplift), erosion (Surtsey), sediment supply (Tuvalu) and ice loading.
notes.quote: Greenland itself will eventually rise up

notes.note: About 3.9 ± 0.4 mm/yr over 1971–2014, or roughly 0.15 m in total. This is the natural experiment: how islands behaved under a known, moderate rise.

notes.note: Headline result. The figure is net: islands gained 80.7 ha and lost 7.24 ha (p. 3). 73.5 ha is 0.735 km², spread over 101 islands.
notes.quote: a net increase in land area in Tuvalu of 73.5 ha

notes.note: The target paradigm. If islands are mobile sediment bodies, a rising sea need not drown them in place. Compare the 'bathtub' maps often used in the media.
notes.quote: flawed assumptions that islands are static landforms

notes.note: The sample is the whole population: every island in the country. Most earlier studies sampled a few islands.
notes.quote: Comprising 9 atolls and 101 individual reef islands

notes.note: Data exercise: in Table 1, Nanumea's change is −1.32 ha on 356.1 ha, which is about −0.37%, but the % column shows −0.004. Also check whether the atoll rows sum to 73.5 ha. By our arithmetic they sum to about 63.1 ha. Work out possible reasons (rounding, island-level aggregation, a typo) before reading on.
Size threshold: the four islands that lost more than half their area all started below 0.5 ha. In this dataset, the smallest motu behave differently from the rest.
notes.quote: erosion was most prevalent on the smallest islands

notes.note: One transect every 10 m (Methods, p. 6). Most islands show erosion on one shore and accretion on another, so islands move as well as change size.

notes.note: Sediment grade matters: 13 of 24 sand islands shrank, while gravel islands mostly grew. These are different landforms with different responses.
notes.quote: of the sand islands reduced in size

notes.note: The key inference. Read it closely: a non-uniform response shows that other processes dominate, not that sea level has no effect. The authors say other processes 'may mask' the sea-level signal.
notes.quote: sea-level change alone cannot account for the observed island changes

notes.note: Storms build as well as destroy. The 1972 cyclone dumped coarse rubble on Funafuti's eastern reef flat, and waves later reworked it onto island shores. Masselink et al. (2020) model this overwash process.

notes.note: Fogafale has 3,427 people/km²; Nanumaga has 183. Here the paper moves from geomorphology to internal migration and land tenure. Compare Baldacchino on who sets the terms.

notes.note: A strong claim. Read the hedge in the same sentence: habitability also depends on fresh water and food. Land area alone does not make an island habitable.

notes.note: Scope limit: the observed rate matches low-emission (RCP2.6) projections. Under high emissions the past four decades are not a reliable guide, so the conclusion is conditional.
